nodes.label: Urban Agglomeration Economies
nodes.rationale: Cities are explained through localised aggregate increasing returns whose benefits must be weighed against urban congestion costs.

nodes.label: Localised Aggregate Increasing Returns
nodes.rationale: Small indivisibilities or other non-convexities must aggregate into city-level increasing returns capable of sustaining cities with trade.

nodes.label: Sharing, Matching, and Learning Taxonomy
nodes.rationale: The taxonomy classifies theories by the mechanism driving agglomeration rather than by the labels assigned to model components.

nodes.label: Sharing Mechanisms
nodes.rationale: Agglomeration can let agents share indivisible facilities, wider input variety, narrower specialisation, and risk.

nodes.label: Matching Mechanisms
nodes.rationale: Agglomeration can improve expected match quality or matching probability and can reduce hold-up problems.

nodes.label: Learning Mechanisms
nodes.rationale: Agglomeration supports knowledge generation, diffusion, and accumulation through interaction and proximity.

nodes.label: Sharing Indivisible Facilities
nodes.rationale: A shared facility spreads a large fixed cost across users while crowding and commuting costs rise with the size of the user community.

nodes.label: City as Spatial Club
nodes.rationale: A city can be understood as a spatial club organised to share a common local public good or facility.

nodes.label: Chamberlinian Input Sharing
nodes.rationale: A larger workforce supports more differentiated intermediate suppliers, allowing final producers to share a wider variety and obtain aggregate increasing returns.

nodes.label: Localisation Economies
nodes.rationale: Proximity to firms in the same sector lowers production costs by making local intermediate suppliers and varieties available.

nodes.label: Urban Specialisation Result
nodes.rationale: With freely traded final goods and locally used intermediate inputs, a small employment shift raises wages in the gaining sector and amplifies full sectoral specialisation.

nodes.label: Efficient City Size
nodes.rationale: Optimal city size balances agglomeration benefits against commuting and crowding costs, and increases with the strength of increasing returns.

nodes.label: City-Creation Coordination Failure
nodes.rationale: Workers would prefer more cities at efficient size but cannot coordinate individually to create them, producing stable cities that are too large.

nodes.label: Gains from Individual Specialisation
nodes.rationale: A larger market lets workers divide labour more finely and spend more time on each task, raising individual productivity.

nodes.label: Labour Pooling
nodes.rationale: Sharing a labour market across firms lets firms absorb idiosyncratic productivity shocks with less wage and employment distortion.

nodes.label: Matching Externality
nodes.rationale: A larger local market improves expected match quality and can also make firm entry reduce fixed costs, although business stealing can create excessive entry.

nodes.label: Increasing-Returns Matching Function
nodes.rationale: More vacancies and job seekers can reduce search frictions, increase matching rates, and make a larger city provide more options while also making agents choosier.

nodes.label: Agglomeration Mitigates Hold-up
nodes.rationale: A city with many alternative partners gives investors an outside option and can make post-investment opportunism less damaging.

nodes.label: Knowledge Generation
nodes.rationale: Diversified cities support experimentation because young firms can test local production processes before relocating to a specialised city.

nodes.label: Nursery Cities
nodes.rationale: Diversified cities are temporary learning environments for firms, while mature firms relocate to cities specialised in their successful process.

nodes.label: Knowledge Diffusion
nodes.rationale: Face-to-face proximity can transmit skills and information, but the chapter notes that detailed micro-foundations for local learning effects remain incomplete.

nodes.label: Knowledge Accumulation
nodes.rationale: Urban growth models add city-level production or learning externalities to equations governing human capital or knowledge accumulation.

nodes.label: Static Externality with Dynamic Effects
nodes.rationale: A static city production externality can simultaneously justify cities and drive sustained growth when output is accumulated as human capital.

nodes.label: Dynamic Human-capital Externality
nodes.rationale: Growth is generated by a learning function in which individual human-capital accumulation depends on the city stock of human capital.

nodes.label: Local Knowledge Spillovers
nodes.rationale: Sustained innovation requires new knowledge to add to an existing stock, with locally scoped spillovers linking urban proximity to growth.

nodes.label: Urban Congestion Costs
nodes.rationale: Commuting, crowding, and land costs counteract local increasing returns and limit efficient city size.

nodes.label: Marshallian Equivalence
nodes.rationale: Different microeconomic mechanisms can produce observationally equivalent urban outcomes even though their market failures and policies differ.

nodes.label: Heterogeneity of Workers and Firms
nodes.rationale: The chapter treats heterogeneity as a root of many agglomeration mechanisms and a central unresolved empirical identification issue.

nodes.label: Incomplete Information
nodes.rationale: Cities help agents find inputs and customers, experiment, and discover possibilities, making agglomeration especially valuable in uncertain environments.

nodes.label: Henderson 1974 Sizes and Types of Cities
Duranton and Puga 2001 Sectoral to Functional Specialisation
From Sectoral to Functional Urban Specialisation
Sectoral Urban Specialisation
nodes.rationale: Cities are specialised in particular sectors when integrated headquarters and production plants share sector-specific localisation economies.

nodes.label: Functional Urban Specialisation
nodes.rationale: Lower remote-management costs allow headquarters and business services to cluster in large cities while production plants cluster in smaller, sector-specialised cities.

nodes.label: Separation of Headquarters and Production
nodes.rationale: Firm organisation and urban structure are jointly determined because separating activities changes both the environments firms seek and the employment patterns that make those environments valuable.

nodes.label: Remote Management Cost
nodes.rationale: Transmission of headquarters services across cities creates an iceberg cost, represented by rho, that determines whether spatial separation is worthwhile.

nodes.label: Sharing Business Service Suppliers
nodes.rationale: Headquarters in different sectors can share a diverse local supply of business services, reducing headquarters costs across sectors.

nodes.label: Sharing Sector-specific Intermediate Suppliers
nodes.rationale: A larger workforce in a sector-specific intermediate industry creates more local varieties and lowers production costs for that final sector.

nodes.label: Headquarters and Business Services
nodes.rationale: Headquarters seek cities with abundant shared business services, so their clustering is cross-sectoral rather than tied to one manufacturing sector.

nodes.label: Production Plants and Sector-specific Intermediates
nodes.rationale: Production plants seek cities with abundant same-sector intermediates, so their clustering remains sector-specific even after headquarters separate.

nodes.label: Urban Congestion Costs
nodes.rationale: Larger cities have higher commuting and living costs, which prevents manufacturing plants with weaker localisation economies from remaining in headquarters cities.

nodes.label: Specialisation by Type of Firm
nodes.rationale: Localisation economies make mixing multi-location headquarters and production plants with integrated firms unattractive to profit-maximising developers.

nodes.label: Three Equilibrium City Types
nodes.rationale: Equilibrium permits headquarters and business-service cities, production-plant and intermediate cities, or integrated-firm cities specialised in one sector.

nodes.label: Remote Management Threshold
nodes.rationale: A threshold comparison of integrated and multi-location unit costs determines the organisational and urban regime.

nodes.label: Large Headquarters and Business-service Cities
nodes.rationale: When business-service localisation economies are stronger than manufacturing localisation economies, headquarters cities are larger.

nodes.label: Small Manufacturing Cities
nodes.rationale: Weaker manufacturing localisation economies and high congestion costs push production into smaller cities.

nodes.label: Transport and Telecommunication Progress
nodes.rationale: Cheaper transport, communication, and improved management practices reduce the cost of coordinating geographically separated facilities.

nodes.label: Business-service Localisation Advantage
nodes.rationale: Stronger localisation economies for business services than for manufacturing increase the size and concentration of headquarters cities.

nodes.label: Davis and Henderson Agglomeration of Headquarters
Note on the Concept of Growth Poles
Growth Poles
nodes.rationale: Growth originates at active poles with unequal intensity and spreads through channels with varied effects on the wider economy.

nodes.label: Uneven Growth and Diffusion
nodes.rationale: Observable growth does not appear everywhere at once; it is concentrated at points or poles and then diffused through prices, flows, and anticipations.

nodes.label: Progressive Industry or Firm
nodes.source_location: Abstract and section on motor industry; lines 40-45 and 227-247
nodes.rationale: A progressive industry grows faster than the surrounding economy for a period and can exercise a motor effect on other industries.

nodes.label: External Economies Beyond Prices
nodes.rationale: Firms can be linked by output, service purchases, and technical change in addition to prices, creating non-Paretian interdependence.

nodes.label: Induced Growth
nodes.rationale: The contribution of a growing industry includes both its own product and the additional product it induces in its environment.

nodes.label: Industrial Centre
nodes.rationale: Industrial centres combine key industries, their environment, and relations among large firms to generate expansive forces across the national economy.

nodes.label: Motor Industry
nodes.source_location: Section on motor industry; lines 227-253 and 513-526
nodes.rationale: A motor industry expands output or lowers prices in ways that induce output and service purchases by other industries.

nodes.label: Key Industry
nodes.rationale: A key industry induces a much larger increase in total output than the increase in its own output, making it a relative analytical category rather than a fixed list of sectors.

nodes.label: Complex of Industries
nodes.rationale: The complex combines a key industry, a non-competitive regime, and territorial agglomeration rather than merely linking industries through prices.

nodes.label: Non-competitive Industrial Complex
nodes.rationale: Oligopolistic suppliers and customers create dynamic price, quantity, cooperation, and conflict relations that can propel wider expansion.

nodes.label: Territorial Agglomeration
nodes.rationale: Geographic concentration adds proximity, contacts, collective needs, skill formation, and interregional disparity to the industry complex.

nodes.label: Proximity and Human Contacts
nodes.rationale: Geographic proximity intensifies economic activity and helps producers, workers, and managers form shared traditions and collective capacities.

nodes.label: Expansive Forces
nodes.source_location: Abstract and section on industrial centres; lines 46-50 and 614-615
nodes.rationale: The combined relations of key industries, large firms, and their environment generate expansion in wider ensembles.

nodes.label: Creative Anticipations and Plans
nodes.source_location: Section on motor industry; lines 335-345 and 413-424
nodes.rationale: New industries emerge when agents form compatible plans and expectations; successful novelty becomes an example that stimulates imitation.

nodes.label: Structural Change
nodes.source_location: Introduction and motor industry section; lines 136-174 and 438-461
nodes.rationale: Observable growth changes industry composition, proportions, linkages, institutions, and the distribution of growth across space.

nodes.label: Active and Passive Economic Sets
nodes.source_location: Growth of poles and national economies; lines 695-704
nodes.rationale: A growing national economy consists of active industries and agglomerated poles that induce growth in relatively passive industries and regions.

nodes.label: Economic Space and National Space Conflict
nodes.source_location: Growth of poles and national economies; lines 709-740
nodes.rationale: The spaces of firms, industries, and poles do not coincide with politically organised national territories, producing conflict between economic and state geographies.

nodes.label: Growth Pole Policy
nodes.rationale: Policy can deliberately form industrial complexes by coupling extraction, energy, transport, and transformation centres.

nodes.label: Spatial Concentration and Transport Links
nodes.rationale: Connecting agglomerated poles through material and intellectual transport routes changes economic horizons and spreads exchange from concentrated points.

nodes.label: Pole Decline and Stagnation
nodes.rationale: Concentrated people, capital, rigid installations, and structures that supported a pole can turn it into a centre of stagnation when its growth declines.

nodes.label: Balanced Growth of the World Economy
nodes.rationale: Growth-pole and national-state arrangements can generate economic waste, motivating coordinated growth policies at the world scale.
